keyVerseText: The children of Keros, the children of Siaha, the children of Padon, Siaha: or, Sia
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun פָּדוֹן (Pâdôwn) derives from the root פָּדָה (pâdâh), which fundamentally means to ransom, redeem, or rescue. This root conveys the idea of severing or releasing someone from bondage or danger, emphasizing deliverance and preservation. Thus, the literal sense of פָּדוֹן goes beyond a simple label and carries the profound concept of redemption and liberation, which enriches its English gloss of 'ransom.'
usageInScripture: The word פָּדוֹן appears only twice in Scripture, both times as a proper name referring to a head of a family among the Nethinim, temple servants who returned with Zerubbabel. Its translation consistently reflects this personal name usage, as seen in the phrase 'of Padon.' This limited occurrence highlights that while the root carries a rich theological meaning, the noun itself in Scripture functions as a designation of a specific individual or family line.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding פָּדוֹן in light of its root meaning 'to ransom' invites reflection on God's redemptive work. Even though here it names a person, the concept of ransom underscores the biblical theme of deliverance central to the Christian faith. Christ's atoning sacrifice is the ultimate ransom, securing freedom from sin and death. Thus, the presence of this word as a name among God's servants reminds believers of their identity as redeemed people called to serve the Lord, reflecting the transformative power of divine redemption.
keyVerseReflection: Ezra 2:44 mentions 'the children of Padon' as part of the returning community, identifying them as descendants of a temple servant family. The use of פָּדוֹן here connects this group to the heritage of redemption and service implicit in the name's root meaning. It reminds readers that those who return to God are part of a redeemed people, called to live in covenant faithfulness and worship.
